designs.name: Editable SQLite
designs.description: Conventional record: rows updated in place, editable status log, unsigned receipts checked against the database

storage.method: SQLite page_count x page_size after a WAL checkpoint (sealed content included)

designs.name: Hardened log
designs.description: Append-only, SHA-256 hash-chained entries signed by the operator (Ed25519); triggers block UPDATE/DELETE; signed receipts

storage.method: SQLite page_count x page_size after a WAL checkpoint (sealed content included)

designs.name: Hardened + checkpoints
designs.description: As hardened, plus the head hash handed to an independent party after every write

storage.method: SQLite page_count x page_size after a WAL checkpoint (sealed content included)

designs.name: VulnSeal (local chain)
designs.description: Contract enforces roles, transitions and arbitration rules; commitments and a hash-chained log on-chain; content sealed off-chain

storage.method: off-chain: SQLite page_count x page_size of the VulnSeal store (sealed reports, reveals, mirror, rationales); on-chain: storage slots per submission from the contract layout (5-slot struct + replay-protection slot + log-entry slot)

scenarios.title: Valid commitment followed by a matching reveal
Reveal containing modified report material
scenarios.attacker: Researcher reveals content edited after committing

editable.note: Commitment check is cryptography, not storage: every design that keeps a commitment detects this

scenarios.title: Operator rewrites a stored commitment so a modified reveal is accepted
scenarios.attacker: Operator with database and signing-key access, colluding with the researcher

hardened.note: The operator holds the signing key, so a consistent rewrite re-signs cleanly

blockchain.note: Verification uses the on-chain commitment; the off-chain edit is also flagged by the audit

scenarios.title: Attempted replacement of an earlier commitment
scenarios.attacker: Researcher replaces a committed report through the normal write path

editable.note: A conventional edit updates the row in place; the earlier commitment is no longer retrievable

hardened.note: Revision is appended; the original entry stays

blockchain.note: reviseCommitment() creates a new commitment; the original keeps its time and can still be opened

scenarios.title: Two reports associated with the same issue family by qualified reviewers
scenarios.attacker: Normal workflow: proposal by one program, independent review by the other

scenarios.title: Two similar-looking reports classified as distinct
scenarios.attacker: Normal workflow; nothing may be merged automatically

blockchain.note: Hashes of similar reports are unrelated; only a reviewed SAME_ISSUE association creates a family token

scenarios.title: Report content disclosed before the process permits it
scenarios.attacker: Reviewer reads before the reveal; researcher reveals before it is requested

editable.note: Enforced by the same application rule in every design; content is sealed at rest in all of them

scenarios.title: Unauthorized attempt to change a recorded decision
scenarios.attacker: Operator edits the decision (and covers its tracks) after arbitration

hardened-anchored.note: Rewriting checkpointed entries breaks the externally held head

blockchain.note: The decision of record is on-chain; editing the off-chain copy is flagged (DISPUTE_MIRROR_ALTERED)

scenarios.title: Dispute followed by a valid appeal
scenarios.attacker: Normal workflow; both rounds must remain retrievable

editable.note: Honest operation keeps the round-1 votes, so both rounds can be reconstructed

scenarios.title: Attempt to hide an earlier status event
scenarios.attacker: Operator removes the record of a failed reveal check

hardened.note: Consistent deletion renumbers and re-signs the log

blockchain.note: The mismatch count and log entry are on-chain; deleting the off-chain copy is flagged (MIRROR_EVENT_MISSING)

scenarios.title: Conflicted or compromised reviewer attempts to adjudicate
scenarios.attacker: Rotates: conflicted arbitrator; duplicate vote; operator-forged vote

editable.note: Conflict and duplicate-vote rules are enforced by every design; only forged attribution separates them

blockchain.note: The operator has no arbitrator's key, so a forged vote cannot be signed

scenarios.title: Receipt presented with missing or mismatched information
scenarios.attacker: Rotates: missing field; altered commitment; holder backdating; operator-issued backdated receipt

editable.note: Unsigned receipts are checked against the operator's own database, so an operator-issued backdated receipt passes

blockchain.note: Block times are set by the chain, not by the record-keeping operator

S11: operator forges a vote in an arbitrator's name

disclosure.item: Dispute existence, votes and reason codes

notes: Measured directly: latency of committing (computing the commitment, sealing the report, recording it; for the blockchain design this includes signing, the RPC round trip and waiting for the receipt), status transitions, reveal checks and receipt verification; throughput = commits / summed commit time for one sequential client; SQLite sizes; gas and calldata from transaction receipts.

Simulated attacks: each scenario is executed against each design and the design's own verifier then runs. P = prevented (the attacker's goal was rejected), D = applied but detected, U = applied and not detected. Functional scenarios report whether the workflow behaved correctly.

Insider model: the operator controls the off-chain database, the evidence store, the vault key and (for the hardened designs) the log-signing key, but not other participants' private keys. The prototype server holds all demo keys for convenience; a deployment must not.
The local Hardhat chain automines each transaction instantly on one node. Real networks add block and consensus latency, so blockchain latencies here are lower bounds.
Blockchain receipt verification makes about a dozen RPC calls to the node; centralised verification is an in-process lookup. The numbers are not like-for-like.
On-chain bytes per submission come from the contract's storage layout, not from node disk usage; per-event on-chain storage is one 32-byte log-entry slot plus state updates.
The disclosure table is computed by scanning the stored data of each design and every transaction input and log on the chain for the synthetic report markers and nonces.
Single run on one machine; results are descriptive. No statistical significance testing was performed; repeat with several seeds to assess variability.
